Heading: Made-in-India Stealth Frigate INS Mahendragiri Joins Navy
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the indigenously built stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy at Visakhapatnam.
• The warship, built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited under Project 17A, enhances India's maritime security and naval-industrial capabilities.
• Rajnath Singh emphasized the integration of modern technology with conventional military power to strengthen India's national security and economic interests.
Content: VISAKHAPATNAM: India took another significant step towards defence self-reliance on Saturday with the commissioning of the indigenously built advanced stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy's Eastern Fleet. The warship was commissioned by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh at Visakhapatnam, who described it as a symbol of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and the country's growing capability to build technologically advanced and combat-ready naval platforms. Built under Project 17A by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL) and designed by the Indian Navy's Warship Design Bureau, INS Mahendragiri is the sixth stealth frigate of the class to be inducted within just one-and-a-half years. With more than 75 per cent indigenous content, the vessel represents one of India's most sophisticated home-built frontline warships. Addressing the commissioning ceremony, Rajnath Singh said INS Mahendragiri reflects India's expanding naval-industrial ecosystem and its ability to design and deliver world-class warships. He said the vessel would strengthen India's maritime security, extend the Navy's blue-water operational reach and reinforce the country's presence across the Indian Ocean Region. The 6,670-tonne stealth frigate is capable of speeds of up to 28 knots and is designed to undertake the full spectrum of maritime operations, including fleet air defence, anti-surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, surveillance and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions. Equipped with advanced stealth features, modern sensors, network-centric combat systems and state-of-the-art weaponry, INS Mahendragiri can be fitted with the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, medium-range surface-to-air missiles, indigenous anti-submarine rocket launchers, torpedo systems, an integrated anti-submarine defence system, electronic warfare suites and close-in weapon systems. The ship also operates an embarked multi-role helicopter, significantly enhancing its combat capability against aerial, surface and underwater threats. Highlighting the evolving nature of warfare, Rajnath Singh said emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, drones, cyber warfare and hypersonic weapons are transforming military operations, but conventional military power continues to remain the backbone of national defence. "Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power," the Defence Minister said, adding that the government remains committed to simultaneously strengthening advanced technologies and conventional defence capabilities. Referring to Operation Sindoor, he said the recent military operation demonstrated the effective integration of modern technology with conventional combat capabilities in safeguarding national security. Emphasising the strategic importance of maritime security, Rajnath Singh reiterated India's commitment to the vision of Security and Growth for All in the Region (SAGAR) and described the Indian Navy as a trusted security partner and first responder in the Indo-Pacific region. He noted that during the recent West Asia conflict, under Operation Urja Suraksha, the Indian Navy safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying essential cargo worth over 9,000 crore, highlighting the force's growing role in protecting India's economic interests in addition to national security. The Defence Minister said indigenous warship construction contributes not only to defence preparedness but also strengthens manufacturing, precision engineering, electronics, software, logistics and other industrial sectors, generating employment and promoting technological innovation.

Heading: Even Caesar did not send a lie to the Senate
Summary:
• Congress seeks privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh for allegedly misleading Parliament regarding Operation Sindoor.
• The article emphasizes that ministers must provide accurate information to Parliament to uphold democratic accountability.
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha may refer the matter to the Committee on Privileges for an official enquiry.
Content: The ensuing Monsoon Session of Parliament is bound to be turbulent, as the Congress seeks privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, alleging that he misled Parliament over Operation Sindoor about the six soldiers who laid their lives in the line of duty. The Speaker, Lok Sabha, may seek the comments of the Minister or refer it to the Committee on Privileges for enquiry and report. The Speaker has the inherent power to close a matter if satisfied with the explanation tendered. The veracity or otherwise of the allegation will be ascertained after due procedural enquiry. However, the central question is what consequences would visit if a minister deliberately misled the Parliament. The veracity of statements made in the legislature by the members, including ministers, is a fundamental postulate of a deliberative democracy. Ordinarily, it is presumed that the statements made or answers given in Parliament are sacrosanct, unless proved otherwise. Parliament can function efficiently and effectively as the supreme deliberative body of the nation if accurate and complete information is furnished to it. The Council of Ministers is accountable to the Parliament and the information that they give to Parliament must be correct and complete, without which the doctrine of accountability would become a myth. Suppression of truth, giving convoluted answers or to mislead Parliament or its committees constitutes a breach of privilege. Therefore, greater responsibility is cast on a minister sworn to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to discharge his duties faithfully and conscientiously as a Minister for the Union. An inaccuracy or chance mistake may inadvertently creep in the statements made or replies given by a minister in Parliament. The Rules of Procedure and Directions of Parliament provide that in case any inaccuracy or mistake is detected in any answer given or statement made by a Minister, the same shall be pointed out as soon as it is detected and the mistake rectified with the permission of the Speaker. There are many instances of the Ministers making the correcting statements, especially of the answers given to questions. But making a misleading statement deliberately or concealing information from Parliament constitutes breach of privilege, unless the Minister invokes the plea of national interest. But making a false or deliberately misleading statement is grossly unethical, against sacrosanct parliamentary conventions and unpardonable. Untruthful or misleading statements undermine parliamentary democracy. 'Satyae Meva Jayatae' and 'Yato dharma tato Jaya' are the foremost ideals of India's great civilisational heritage. Many consider India as the mother of Democracy, and justifiably, with reference to Vedic texts and post-Vedic literature. The Indian civilisational texts of great antiquity lay immense stress on truth and righteousness. There are inscriptions in the old Parliament Building taken from the Mahabharata and the Manusmriti reminding that members of the Assembly must speak with righteousness, and the righteousness must be based on truth, and truth is not truth if it leads to deceit.

Visakhapatnam: Union defence minister Rajnath Singh said the nature of warfare is changing rapidly, and future wars may be fought with artificial intelligence (AI), but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power. The Indian Navy on Saturday inducted the indigenously built advanced stealth frigate 'INS Mahendragiri' into its Eastern Fleet during a ceremony presided over by Rajnath Singh in Visakhapatnam. Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, Singh emphasised that while emerging technologies such as drones, AI, cyber warfare, space-based capabilities, hypersonic weapons and unmanned systems have transformed warfare, conventional military capabilities continue to form the bedrock of effective defence. "Future wars may be fought with AI, but they will still be won by soldiers and capable military power," he said, stressing that advanced technologies and conventional platforms complement one another. He said Andhra Pradesh has emerged as a new powerhouse of India's defence and aerospace manufacturing, with Kurnool set to emerge as India's drone hub on the lines of Surat as Diamond City and Bengaluru as Silicon Valley. INS Mahendragiri reflects India's growing self-reliance in shipbuilding, underpinned by design capabilities, manufacturing excellence, growth of the naval-industrial ecosystem, and timely delivery of state-of-the-art platforms. It is the sixth Project 17A indigenous stealth frigate inducted into the Navy in just 18 months. The first ship 'INS Nilgiri' was commissioned in Jan 2025, followed by 'INS Udaygiri' and 'INS Himgiri' in Aug, 'INS Taragiri' in April this year and 'INS Dunagiri' last month. Designed by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL), Mumbai, the ship can undertake fleet air defence, anti-surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, surveillance and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR). "INS Mahendragiri can be equipped with the BrahMos surface-to-surface missile, one of the world's fastest and most lethal cruise missiles. It also features multifunction radar and surface-to-air missiles capable of detecting and neutralising aerial threats at extended ranges. Its arsenal includes an indigenous rocket launcher, torpedo launchers, an integrated anti-submarine defence system, an electronic warfare suite and a close-in weapon system. All these capabilities make the warship formidable and resilient," Singh said. He voiced the government's commitment to maintaining a balanced approach by investing in next-generation technologies while strengthening conventional capabilities. "Operation Sindoor was a prime example of effective integration of conventional and modern capabilities to safeguard national security," he said, adding that INS Mahendragiri symbolises the nation's commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy. He asserted that maritime and economic security are closely linked, with the seas vital to national security, trade, supply chains, energy security, and economic growth. Highlighting the Indo-Pacific's strategic importance, he reaffirmed his commitment to the vision of Security and Growth for All in the Region (SAGAR). Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan termed INS Mahendragiri a symbol of India's growing maritime capabilities and technological self-reliance.

It is playing its role across air, water, land, and the unmanned domain,” he remarked, adding, “This means the weapon systems that we once used to import from abroad will now be produced near our own Vizag,” he said. He cited the foundation stone laying for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) Core Integration and Flight Testing Centre at Puttaparthi and Bharat Dynamics Limited’s upcoming Naval Systems Manufacturing Facility in Anakapalli, where autonomous underwater vehicles, torpedoes and underwater countermeasure systems will be produced. “AMCA in the skies, BDL’s naval systems in the depths of the ocean, Kurnool’s drones in the unmanned domain, and today, INS Mahendragiri on the surface of the sea signify that Andhra Pradesh is now contributing to India’s defence strength across every sphere,” he noted. The Defence Minister also underlined the changing character of warfare, observing that technological advances were transforming military operations without diminishing the importance of conventional capabilities. “Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power,” he remarked. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, drones, cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons and space-based systems, he emphasised, complement rather than replace conventional military platforms. Citing Operation Sindoor, the Defence Minister pointed to the operation as an illustration of the effective integration of modern technologies with conventional military capability. The frigate was designed by the Indian Navy’s Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited, Mumbai. With over 75% indigenous content, the 6,670-tonne warship can attain 28 knots. It is configured for fleet air defence, anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, surveillance and HADR. It carries supersonic and medium-range missiles, stealth features, sensors, network-centric systems, anti-submarine weapons and a multi-role helicopter. It could also be equipped with the BrahMos missile system. Describing maritime security as integral to India’s economic interests, the Defence Minister observed that secure sea lanes were essential for trade, energy security and resilient supply chains. He noted that the Indian Navy’s humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and evacuation missions had reinforced its role as a first responder and a preferred security partner in the Indo-Pacific. Referring to Operation Urja Suraksha during the West Asia conflict, he stated that the Navy had safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying cargo worth more than ₹9,000 crore. Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan described INS Mahendragiri as another milestone in indigenously built warship construction that would strengthen the Navy’s operational capability. Built with contributions from more than 200 Indian industries, including several MSMEs, the frigate is named after the Mahendragiri mountain range in the Eastern Ghats and will enhance the Navy’s operational reach in the Indian Ocean Region.

• J&K Police confiscated the property of terrorist Ghulam Mohammad Bhat in Sopore.
• PM Narendra Modi highlighted India's military strength and defense capabilities, specifically citing 'Operation Sindoor' during his visit to Australia.
Content: Islamabad (Agency). A commander of the terrorist organization Hizbul Mujahideen has made a big confession on camera regarding Pakistan's misdeeds. Actually, a video of Hizbul's Deputy Supreme Commander Shamsheer Khan has recently surfaced. In this video, the terrorist is seen confessing on camera that terrorists from every corner of Pakistan tried to create terror in Kashmir and were killed at the hands of security forces. Shamsheer openly confessed that there is no graveyard left in Kashmir where the bodies of Pakistani terrorists are not buried. While addressing a meeting of Jamaat-e-Islami organized in Muzaffarabad, Pakistan-occupied Kashmir last July, Shamsheer Khan said that from Lolab and Kupwara to Kathua, there is not a single graveyard in Kashmir where Pakistani terrorists are not buried. The Hizbul terrorist did not stop here. After this confession, Shamsheer talked about the relationship between Pakistan and Kashmir and claimed that no one can create hatred between them. He also said that this statement of Khan confirms India's claim of how Pakistan uses its nurtured terrorists to spread terror in Kashmir. India itself has been providing evidence for this from time to time. Target on Hizbul Terrorist: It is noteworthy that this video has come at a time when just last May, the Jammu and Kashmir Police had confiscated the property of Ghulam Mohammad Bhat alias Haider, an active Hizbul Mujahideen terrorist from Panjla, Sopore. According to the police, Haider had fled to PoK for training in illegal weapons and was carrying out terrorist activities against India from there. PM Modi recalled Operation Sindoor: On one hand, while Pakistani terrorists are mourning their deaths in the valley, on the other hand, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has proved the mettle of India's military capabilities during his Australia visit. Speaking at an event for the Indian diaspora in Australia, PM Modi specifically mentioned Operation Sindoor. During this, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was also present on the stage. Praising India's defense systems and the major actions taken against terrorism, PM Modi said, today the whole world is seeing the capability and reliability of India's defense platforms. You must have seen a big demonstration of this during Operation Sindoor.

Heading: AI may shape future wars, but victory will depend on soldiers, national resolve: Rajnath Singh
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Visakhapatnam.
• He emphasized balancing Artificial Intelligence with conventional military strength for national security.
• Singh highlighted the 'Maritime India Vision 2030' to boost indigenous shipbuilding, economic growth, and India's global standing in maritime innovation.
Content: Visakhapatnam, July 11 (IANS) Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday asserted that while emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence are transforming the nature of warfare, conventional military capabilities remain indispensable, stressing that future conflicts may involve AI but will ultimately be won through national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military strength. Addressing the gathering during the commissioning ceremony of INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Andhra Pradesh's Visakhapatnam, Defence Minister Singh said, "While new technologies have certainly transformed the nature of warfare, they have not diminished the importance of conventional warfare capabilities. Strong conventional capabilities remain just as essential today as ever for fulfilling the fundamental principles of warfare. Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won through national resolve, trained soldiers, and credible military power." Highlighting the need to balance technological advancement with conventional strength, the Defence Minister said, "New technology and conventional platforms are not adversaries but complements to one another; a conventional platform is incomplete without new technology, and a conventional platform is weakened without it. History bears witness that nations which neglected their conventional strength, lured by the appeal of new technology, had to pay a heavy price." Emphasising India's long-term defence strategy, Defence Minister Singh said, "Therefore, India's approach is very clear: We must excel in both areas and maintain a balance between them." "We will invest in future technologies while continuously honing our conventional capabilities. INS Mahendragiri stands as a symbol of this very resolve and commitment," he added. Referring to India's recent military operations, the Defence Minister said the country's ability to effectively integrate conventional and modern capabilities had already been demonstrated. "In recent times, we have also witnessed how our conventional and modern capabilities work in tandem when it comes to national security. 'Operation Sindoor' was a prime example of this. During that operation, our armed forces demonstrated that India is fully capable not only of self-defence but also of delivering a decisive response and completely eliminating the enemy when the need arises," he said. Defence Minister Singh further stated that every warship commissioned into the Navy contributes to strengthening India's broader defence and industrial ecosystem. "With every ship, India's ecosystem matures, becomes more efficient, and grows more confident." Explaining the wider economic significance of indigenous warship construction, he said, "That is why I believe that every new ship represents a long-term investment in India's maritime future. The construction of a warship is not merely the building of a vessel; it entails the creation of an entire industrial ecosystem." "The shipbuilding industry drives progress across sectors such as steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering, logistics, and numerous ancillary industries. This generates employment opportunities for lakhs of people, fosters the development of new technologies, and imparts fresh momentum to our economy. Thus, when we build a ship, we not only strengthen our Navy but also infuse new energy into India's economic prowess," he added. The Defence Minister also said India has an ambitious pipeline of naval projects planned for the coming years, with the objective of positioning the country as a global centre for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation. "I am confident that, in the near future, our country will carve a distinct niche for itself among the world's leading nations in this sector. We aim to move forward in collaboration with domestic industries, the private sector, MSMEs, startups, innovators, and our global partners. Driven by this vision, our government is working rapidly on the 'Maritime India Vision 2030'," he said. He further highlighted the government's policy initiatives aimed at strengthening the maritime sector. "The government has launched several significant initiatives, such as the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme, and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme. These efforts will strengthen our industrial base, expand our shipbuilding capacity, and correspondingly bolster our maritime capabilities to safeguard India's growing economic interests," Singh added.

Heading: India will decide the direction of the ocean: Rajnath Singh
Summary:
• Defense Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the indigenous stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam.
• He emphasized that India is developing capabilities to influence maritime security and project power globally.
• The warship, equipped with BrahMos missiles, represents India's commitment to balancing modern technology with conventional military strength.
Content: Agency ■ Visakhapatnam. Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said that India will no longer just decide its direction through the sea, but is also developing the capacity to decide the direction of the sea. While addressing the soldiers at the commissioning ceremony of the Indian Navy's most advanced warship INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam, he said that India has so far decided its direction through the sea, but now India is going to decide the direction of the sea. According to Rajnath Singh, the Indian Navy's indigenous stealth frigate Mahendragiri is a blue-water ship, meaning it can protect India's maritime interests not only near the coast but also far away in deep oceans for weeks. Our country India has so far decided its direction through the sea, but now our country is also developing the capacity to decide the direction of the sea. The Defense Minister, without naming the America-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, said that new technologies have definitely changed the nature of war, but the importance of conventional war has not diminished. The basic principles of war, to fulfill them, we will invest in strong techniques and will continue to sharpen our conventional capabilities. According to Singh, INS Mahendragiri is a symbol of this resolve and commitment. This means that new technologies like AI or drones and conventional platforms like fighter jets and warships are not against each other, but complementary. Mention of Operation Sindoor: While mentioning Operation Sindoor, Rajnath Singh said that we have also seen in recent times that when it comes to the country's security, our traditional and modern capabilities work together. Our army showed during Operation Sindoor that India is now fully capable of not only defending itself but also giving a decisive answer and destroying enemies when needed. Most lethal supersonic cruise missile: Equipped with the world's fastest and most lethal supersonic cruise missile BrahMos, Mahendragiri is the sixth and final warship of the Navy's Project 17A. Under this project, four warships were built at Mazagon Dockyard Limited in Mumbai and two (02) at Garden Reach Shipbuilders in Kolkata.

Heading: Future wars will still be won by resolve and soldiers, not just AI: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the indigenous warship INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.
• He emphasized that while AI is important, national resolve and conventional military strength remain vital for India's defence.
• The event highlighted India's growing indigenous shipbuilding capabilities and the government's commitment to the SAGAR vision for maritime security.
Content: PRESS TRUST OF INDIA Visakhapatnam, July 11 (PTI) Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and robust military power, Defence Minister Rajanth Singh said on Saturday. Speaking at the commissioning ceremony of INS Mahendragiri here, Singh also said Andhra Pradesh has emerged as a new powerhouse of India’s defence and aerospace manufacturing. Highlighting the government’s balanced approach towards defence modernisation, Singh said India is investing in next-generation technologies while simultaneously strengthening conventional military capabilities. He cited Operation Sindoor as an example of the effective integration of conventional and modern capabilities to safeguard national security. “Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and the capable military power. So, I would say that new technologies and conventional platforms are not opposed to each other, but supplement each other, complete each other. Without conventional platforms, new technologies are incomplete in themselves,” he said. According to Singh, it is certain that new technologies have reshaped warfare, but they have not diminished the role of conventional military means. The strong conventional capability that is still necessary for the fulfilment of basic principles of war is as important as it was before. Emphasising that maritime security and economic security are closely interconnected, Singh said the seas remain vital for trade, supply chains, energy security and economic growth. He reaffirmed the government’s commitment to the Security and Growth for All in the Region (SAGAR) vision in the Indo-Pacific. Calling India a net security provider and trusted regional partner, Singh said the Indian Navy has consistently demonstrated its commitment through humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations, anti-piracy missions and the evacuation of Indian and foreign nationals from conflict-hit regions, earning recognition as both a first responder and a preferred security partner. Referring to the Indian Navy’s role during the recent West Asia conflict, Singh said under Operation Urja Suraksha, the Navy safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying essential cargo valued at more than Rs 9,000 crore, highlighting its role in protecting not only national security but also India’s economic interests. The defence minister said the successful induction of the warship demonstrates India’s growing capability to design, build and deploy complex frontline combat platforms through indigenous expertise. The warship is equipped with an indigenous rocket launcher, torpedo launchers, an Integrated Anti-Submarine Defence System, an Electronic Warfare suite and a Close-In Weapon System, making it a formidable and resilient combat platform capable of operating in challenging maritime environments. Describing INS Mahendragiri as a “blue-water warship”, Singh said it can effectively counter threats from the air, enemy vessels on the surface and submarines hidden beneath the sea, and can protect India’s maritime interests not only near the coastline but also in distant and deep oceans during prolonged deployments. The union minister said the commissioning of Mahendragiri comes at a time when the nature of warfare is rapidly evolving with the emergence of drones, artificial intelligence, cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons, space-based capabilities and unmanned systems. However, he stressed that conventional military capabilities continue to remain the bedrock of effective national defence. The Union Minister described INS Mahendragiri as a symbol of the nation’s commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy capable of meeting future security challenges while protecting India’s maritime interests. He expressed confidence that INS Mahendragiri would further strengthen India’s maritime strategy by enhancing the security of the eastern seaboard, extending the country’s blue-water operational reach and reinforcing its presence across the Indian Ocean Region. Singh said indigenous warship construction goes beyond building combat platforms as it strengthens design capability, technological expertise, skilled manpower and the broader maritime industrial ecosystem. He noted that shipbuilding supports sectors including steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering and logistics while generating employment and fostering innovation. Reiterating the government’s vision to establish India as a global hub for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation, the Union Minister said initiatives such as Maritime India Vision 2030, the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme are aimed at modernising ports, expanding inland waterways, strengthening logistics networks, enhancing industrial capacity and boosting self-reliance. He also called upon young entrepreneurs, engineers, innovators, researchers and investors to contribute to nation-building by developing advanced technologies and defence systems that should shape future warfare and strengthen India’s self-reliance in the defence sector. Singh said the induction of Mahendragiri marks another milestone in India’s journey towards defence self-reliance and strengthens the Navy’s operational capability in safeguarding the country’s maritime interests across the Indian Ocean Region and beyond. The warship is equipped with an indigenous rocket launcher, torpedo launchers, an Integrated Anti-Submarine Defence System, an Electronic Warfare suite and a Close-In Weapon System, making it a formidable and resilient combat platform capable of operating in challenging maritime environments.

Heading: INS Mahendragiri joins Navy’s Eastern Fleet, Defence Minister calls it symbol of India's maritime self-reliance
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the indigenously built stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy's Eastern Fleet at Visakhapatnam.
• The warship, built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited, enhances India's maritime security and self-reliance in defence manufacturing.
• Rajnath Singh emphasized that conventional military power remains essential alongside advanced technologies like AI for national security.
Content: GK News Service Visakhapatnam, Jul 11 Navy on Saturday inducted the indigenously built stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy's Eastern Fleet, with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh describing the frontline warship as a testament to the country's growing self-reliance in defence manufacturing and a major boost to maritime security in the Indo-Pacific. Commissioning the warship at Visakhapatnam, Rajnath Singh said the induction reflected India's "exceptional design capabilities, manufacturing excellence, the rapid growth of the naval-industrial ecosystem, and its ability to deliver state-of-the-art platforms in a timely manner." INS Mahendragiri is the sixth Project 17A stealth frigate to be inducted into the Navy in just 18 months. Designed by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited, the frigate has more than 75 per cent indigenous content and is capable of undertaking the full spectrum of maritime operations, including air defence, anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare, surveillance, maritime interdiction and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions. Highlighting the ship's capabilities, Rajnath Singh said INS Mahendragiri can be equipped with the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile and advanced air-defence systems. "INS Mahendragiri can be equipped with the BrahMos surface-to-surface missile, one of the world's fastest and most lethal cruise missiles. It also features a combination of multifunction radar and Surface-to-Air Missiles capable of detecting and neutralising aerial threats at extended ranges," he said. The Defence Minister said the warship's indigenous rocket launchers, torpedo launchers, integrated anti-submarine defence system, electronic warfare suite and close-in weapon system made it "formidable and resilient". Expressing confidence in the Navy's latest addition, he said the "blue-water ship" would safeguard India's maritime interests "not just near the coast but far out in the deep oceans as well." Referring to the changing character of warfare, Rajnath Singh stressed that while technologies such as artificial intelligence, drones, cyber capabilities, hypersonic weapons and unmanned systems were reshaping battlefields, conventional military power remained indispensable. "Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power," he said. He added that Operation Sindoor had demonstrated the effective integration of conventional military capabilities with advanced technologies and described INS Mahendragiri as another symbol of India's commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy. Emphasising the strategic importance of the seas, Rajnath Singh said maritime security and economic security were inseparable, with secure sea lanes critical for trade, supply chains and energy security. Heading: Tech may shape wars, but resolve wins them: Rajnath
Summary: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the INS Mahendragiri frigate in Visakhapatnam. He emphasized that while AI and technology are crucial, national resolve and trained soldiers remain vital for victory. He highlighted Andhra Pradesh's growing role as a defense manufacturing hub and reaffirmed India's commitment to maritime security and self-reliance under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision.
Content: Defence Minister commissions the stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri, saying future wars may rely on AI and advanced technologies but will ultimately be won by trained soldiers, national resolve and strong conventional military power. Notes AP is emerging as a key defence and aerospace manufacturing hub. Stresses that INS Mahendragiri will strengthen India's maritime security and blue-water capabilities. RANI DEVALLA VISAKHAPATNAM. EVEN as emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, cyber warfare, drone technology, space-based capabilities, unmanned systems and hypersonic weapons have largely transformed the crux of warfare, conventional military capabilities continue to hold sway as far as effective defence is concerned, emphasised Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. Presiding over the commissioning ceremony of the mission-primed INS Mahendragiri, the sixth in the Project 17A Nilgiri-class stealth frigate series, as chief guest at the Naval Dockyard in Visakhapatnam on July 11 (Saturday), the Defence Minister stated, 'Future wars may be fought with AI, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power.' The Defence Minister underlined that Andhra Pradesh is serving as a major hub for the country's defence ecosystem and is steadily emerging as a new powerhouse for defence and aerospace manufacturing in the country. 'In Anakapalli, the foundation stone was laid for the new naval systems manufacturing facility of Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL), while Core Integration and Flight Testing Centre to develop the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft and other indigenous platforms in Puttaparthi. Weapon systems that we earlier used to import will now be manufactured in AP,' the Defence Minister stressed, adding that AP is contributing to India's defence might across air, water, land and unmanned domains. Despite the emerging warfare technologies, Rajnath Singh underlined that advanced technologies and conventional platforms complement one another and exhorted young entrepreneurs, engineers, innovators and researchers to contribute to nation-building by developing technologies that reshape the future course of warfare and make India self-reliant. Highlighting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision to maintain a balanced approach of investing in next-generation technologies and strengthening its conventional might, Rajnath Singh recalled, 'Operation Sindoor was a prime example of the effective integration of conventional and modern capabilities to safeguard national security.' Asserting that maritime and economic securities are closely linked, the Defence Minister mentioned that the seas are vital not only for national security but also for trade, supply chains, energy security and economic growth. 'India is a net security provider and a trusted partner dedicated to ensuring security and development across the region,' he highlighted, praising the Indian Navy for demonstrating this commitment through its role in HADR operations, anti-piracy missions, among a host of others. About the Indian Navy's role during the West Asia conflict, the Defence Minister recalled that under the operation 'Urja Suraksha', Indian Navy safely escorted 18 merchant vessels, carrying essential cargo valued Rs.9,000 crore and stressed on the navy's role as a key protector of India's economic interests. The Defence Minster expressed confidence that INS Mahendragiri will further strengthen the overall maritime strategy of the eastern seaboard, expanding India's blue-water reach and its presence in the Indian Ocean Region. 'Indigenous warship construction stretches beyond creating combat platforms as it strengthens design capabilities, technological expertise, skilled manpower and world class maritime ecosystem. INS Mahendragiri is a symbol of the nation's commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready navy,' Rajnath Singh highlighted, emphasising that apart from producing indigenous ships, Indian shipyards are also catering to foreign countries' needs. Defining INS Mahendragiri as the concluding 'jewel' of Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited's Project 17A programme, the Defence Minister exuded confidence that the frontline warship is certain to boost the Indian Navy's multi-mission capabilities.

The warship is equipped with an indigenous rocket launcher, torpedo launchers, an Integrated Anti-Submarine Defence System, an Electronic Warfare suite and a Close-In Weapon System, making it a formidable and resilient combat platform capable of operating in challenging maritime environments. However, he stressed that conventional military capabilities continue to remain the bedrock of effective national defence. The Union Minister described INS Mahendragiri as a symbol of the nation's commitment to building a technologically advanced and combat-ready Navy capable of meeting future security challenges while protecting India's maritime interests. He expressed confidence that INS Mahendragiri would further strengthen India's maritime strategy by enhancing the security of the eastern seaboard, extending the country's blue-water operational reach and reinforcing its presence across the Indian Ocean Region. Singh said indigenous warship construction goes beyond building combat platforms as it strengthens design capability, technological expertise, skilled manpower and the broader maritime industrial ecosystem. He noted that shipbuilding supports sectors including steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering and logistics while generating employment and fostering innovation. Reiterating the government's vision to establish India as a global hub for shipbuilding and maritime defence innovation, the Union Minister said initiatives such as Maritime India Vision 2030, the Maritime Development Fund, the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme are aimed at modernising ports, expanding inland waterways, strengthening logistics networks, enhancing industrial capacity and boosting self-reliance. He also called upon young entrepreneurs, engineers, innovators, researchers and investors to contribute to nation-building by developing advanced technologies and defence systems that would shape future warfare and strengthen India's self-reliance in the defence sector. Singh said the induction of Mahendragiri marks another milestone in India's journey towards defence self-reliance and strengthens the Navy's operational capability in safeguarding the country's maritime interests across the Indian Ocean Region. Content: New Delhi,11/7: The Hizbul Mujahideen, once projected as a home-grown terror outfit in Jammu and Kashmir, has recently begun changing its strategy.The group, which had remained largely inactive after Indian security forces dismantled most of its networks in Jammu and Kashmir, has now launched a fresh recruitment drive.An Intelligence Bureau official said that the recruitment pattern is, however, different and today the Hizbul Mujahideen has more Pakistani fighters as compared to the local Kashmiris.“This clearly shows that the local Kashmiris no longer want to be part of this outfit; hence a decision to recruit Pakistanis in large numbers has been taken,” the official said.The official said that on July 8, a meeting was held to commemorate the death anniversary of slain Hizbul Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani.The members of the outfit, which is headquartered in Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), discussed a range of issues that involved recruitment and strategy. The Hizbul Mujahideen has been under immense pressure from the Pakistani establishment to regroup and commence operations in Jammu and Kashmir.Post Operation Sindoor, the Hizbul Mujahideen has remained relatively quiet and not focused on its future operations. With the Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) down owing to its top leaders missing in action, the emphasis to commence operations in Jammu and Kashmir largely falls on the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and Hizbul Mujahideen.“The Pakistani establishment is engaging the Lashkar-e-Taiba in the various trouble-torn regions in Pakistan. The terror group has been tasked with taking on outfits such as the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP),” another official said.

Heading: AI may shape future wars, but victory will depend on soldiers: Rajnath
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Visakhapatnam.
• He emphasized that while AI is transforming warfare, victory depends on conventional military strength and trained soldiers.
• Singh highlighted that indigenous warship construction strengthens India's defence, industrial ecosystem, and economic growth.
Content: VISAKHAPATNAM: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday asserted that while emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence are transforming the nature of warfare, conventional military capabilities remain indispensable, stressing that future conflicts may involve AI but will ultimately be won through national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military strength. Addressing the gathering during the commissioning ceremony of INS Mahendragiri into the Indian Navy in Andhra Pradesh's Visakhapatnam, Defence Minister Singh said, "While new technologies have certainly transformed the nature of warfare, they have not diminished the importance of conventional warfare capabilities. Strong conventional capabilities remain just as essential today as ever for fulfilling the fundamental principles of warfare. Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won through national resolve, trained soldiers, and credible military power." Highlighting the need to balance technological advancement with conventional strength, the Defence Minister said, "New technology and conventional platforms are not adversaries but complements to one another; a conventional platform is incomplete without new technology, and a conventional platform is weakened without it. History bears witness that nations which neglected their conventional strength, lured by the appeal of new technology, had to pay a heavy price." Emphasising India's long-term defence strategy, Defence Minister Singh said, "Therefore, India's approach is very clear: We must excel in both areas and maintain a balance between them." "We will invest in future technologies while continuously honing our conventional capabilities. INS Mahendragiri stands as a symbol of this very resolve and commitment," he added. Referring to India's recent military operations, the Defence Minister said the country's ability to effectively integrate conventional and modern capabilities had already been demonstrated. "In recent times, we have also witnessed how our conventional and modern capabilities work in tandem when it comes to national security. 'Operation Sindoor' was a prime example of this. During that operation, our armed forces demonstrated that India is fully capable not only of self-defence but also of delivering a decisive response and completely eliminating the enemy when the need arises," he said. Defence Minister Singh further stated that every warship commissioned into the Navy contributes to strengthening India's broader defence and industrial ecosystem. "With every ship, India's ecosystem matures, becomes more efficient, and grows more confident." Explaining the wider economic significance of indigenous warship construction, he said, "That is why I believe that every new ship represents a long-term investment in India's maritime future. The construction of a warship is not merely the building of a vessel; it entails the creation of an entire industrial ecosystem." "The shipbuilding industry drives progress across sectors such as steel, electronics, sensors, propulsion systems, software, precision engineering, logistics, and numerous ancillary industries. This generates employment opportunities for lakhs of people, fosters the development of new technologies, and imparts fresh momentum to our economy. Thus, when we build a ship, we not only strengthen our Navy but also infuse new energy into India's economic prowess," he added.

He reaffirmed India's commitment to the SAGAR vision and its role as a net security provider, highlighting the Navy's vital contribution to protecting national and economic interests.
Content:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri in Visakhapatnam, marking a significant milestone in India’s maritime capabilities. During the ceremony, Singh emphasized that while Artificial Intelligence and next-generation technologies are reshaping modern warfare, future conflicts will ultimately be won by national resolve, trained soldiers, and robust conventional military power. He asserted that new technologies and conventional platforms are not mutually exclusive but rather supplement and complete each other.

Highlighting the government’s strategic approach, Singh noted that India is simultaneously investing in advanced tech and strengthening traditional military assets. He pointed to Operation Sindoor as a prime example of this effective integration. Furthermore, he identified Andhra Pradesh as an emerging powerhouse for India’s defence and aerospace manufacturing sectors.

Addressing the broader geopolitical landscape, Singh underscored the vital link between maritime and economic security, reaffirming India’s commitment to the SAGAR vision in the Indo-Pacific. He lauded the Indian Navy for its role as a net security provider and a trusted regional partner, citing its humanitarian efforts and anti-piracy missions. Specifically, he highlighted the success of Operation Urja Suraksha, where the Navy safely escorted 18 merchant vessels carrying essential cargo worth over Rs 9,000 crore during the recent West Asia conflict, demonstrating its critical role in protecting both national security and economic interests.

Heading: Navy commissions sixth stealth frigate INS Mahendragiri in 18 months, build time halved
Summary:
• Defence Minister Rajnath Singh commissioned the sixth Project 17A stealth frigate, INS Mahendragiri, in Visakhapatnam.
• Built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, the warship features 75% indigenous content and advanced weaponry.
• The Indian Navy aims to enhance maritime security and regional stability in the Indian Ocean, with Admiral Krishna Swaminathan highlighting improved construction timelines.
Content: NEW DELHI: The Navy on Saturday commissioned INS Mahendragiri at Visakhapatnam, its sixth new-generation Project 17A stealth frigate, in just 18 months period. The 6,670-tonne warship was delivered in 31 months, while similar frigates took 63 months earlier, indicating that the country's warship-building assembly lines are striding ahead at a vital pace. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, presiding over the ceremony, said the frigate will safeguard India's maritime interests not just near the coast but also in the deep oceans. Kitted with BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles, medium-range surface-to-air missiles paired with multifunction radars, torpedo tubes and anti-submarine rocket launchers, an electronic warfare suite and a multi-role helicopter, the 28-knot frigate has over 75 per cent indigenous content. It was designed in-house by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau and built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MDL). Mahendragiri is the sixth of the seven 'Nilgiri-class' frigates. The six being Nilgiri, Udaygiri, Himgiri, Taragiri and Dunagiri. With Vindhyagiri, the seventh frigate in line, the Rs 45,000 crore project will be completed. Navy's new chief, Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, said the halving of launch-to-delivery timelines for the class has come alongside a 20 per cent cut in overall construction time, from 95 to 75 months. Notably, Mahendragiri wrapped up all technical evaluations in a single sea trial, against the usual five to seven. Sources in the defence and security establishments further said that four more ships are slated for delivery to the Navy over the next two months. "The target for 2026 is to commission at least 18 vessels, including the Project 17A frigate, anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft (ASW-SWC), the diving support vessel Nipun and other auxiliary vessels," they said. The compressed timelines are significant for a Force that has long been plagued by tardy deliveries from defence shipyards. China, with the world's largest Navy at over 370 warships and counting, adds new hulls at an unprecedented pace, even as its research vessels and submarines foray into the Indian Ocean Region. Significantly, Rajnath Singh dwelt on the changing character of warfare, stating that even if drones, AI, cyber and hypersonic weapons have transformed conflict, conventional capabilities remain the bedrock of defence. "Future wars may be fought with Artificial Intelligence, but they will still be won by national resolve, trained soldiers and credible military power," he said, citing Operation Sindoor as proof of the two working in tandem. "The Navy's escort of 18 merchant vessels carrying cargo worth over Rs 9,000 crore during the West Asia conflict, under Operation Urja Suraksha, showed the Force was a 'First Responder and Preferred Security Partner' in the Indo-Pacific," he added. The Minister had set the stage a day earlier, highlighting 'Barakhana' in Vizag, that "India stands as the primary guarantor of peace and stability in the Indian Ocean Region," through which over 90 per cent of the country's trade by volume flows. "The region is our courtyard, and securing the courtyard is our responsibility," he said. Cautioning that future conflicts could erupt 'without a formal declaration of war,' Singh promised troops the world's best weaponry. However, he also stated that weapons alone do not win wars, and it is the people who wield them that do.

Heading: This sacrifice should not go in vain
Summary: Prof. Dr. Girish Naik honors the six Indian military personnel martyred during the 2025 'Operation Sindoor' against cross-border terrorism. The Indian government has officially recognized these soldiers by engraving their names at the National War Memorial in New Delhi, acknowledging their supreme sacrifice for the nation.
Content: On the midnight of May 6-7, 2025, the Indian Armed Forces conducted a military operation codenamed 'Operation Sindoor', involving all three wings of the armed forces. The objective was to neutralize the operational capabilities of groups responsible for cross-border terrorism on Indian soil by targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Although reports and information regarding military casualties during the four-day conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025 were available, the government had not officially released information about the soldiers martyred during Operation Sindoor until now. After a year, the government has officially released the names of the six Indian military personnel who were martyred. The names of these soldiers have been included in the martyr's register on the official website of the National War Memorial and have also been engraved on the memorial in New Delhi. Each martyr of Operation Sindoor had their own unique, heart-wrenching story. Someone was an only son, someone was about to get married, someone was near military retirement, and someone was expecting a new arrival in their family. The supreme sacrifice made by these brave soldiers while protecting the nation must be expressed with due respect, gratitude, and honor. It is important to ensure that the sacrifice of the soldiers is the supreme service to the motherland and will always be remembered with full respect, pride, and honor. - Prof. Dr. Girish Naik, Kolhapur. Hallelujah! At least one global person was home and dry even if the world was crying “foul”. President Donald Trump getting the Fifa boss man to revoke a “red card” during Fifa's fiercely fought World Cup football matches has created a permanent black mark on the reputation of the Beautiful Game. In US striker Folarin's place, any other sportsman would have felt humiliated about the embarrassing intervention by no less a person than the President of the country. This is only the second time in World Cup history that Fifa has overturned a suspension for a player sent off during the tournament. Even worse, Gianni Infantino, Fifa's president, should have resigned from his position, rather than surrender to a bully. Tell the world, Signor Infantino, now that you've been stripped of all authority and dignity... how will you appear in history? And please... how are you living with yourself after such a public disgrace? But guess who had the last laugh? Belgium! Didn't you love the way the team mocked President Trump after their win over the United States? So... who are you betting on, folks? Like the rest of the football crazy world, I am crushing on the Viral Viking. Seven goals in four games so far. And that hair... uff... Haaland is Samson! Heading: India sets a target of Rs 50,000 crore in defense exports by the year 2030
Summary:
• Union Defense Minister Rajnath Singh announced India achieved record defense exports of Rs 38,424 crore in FY 2025-26.
• India aims for Rs 50,000 crore in defense exports by 2030 under PM Narendra Modi's leadership.
• The Ministry of Defense successfully utilized its entire Rs 1.86 lakh crore capital budget for the second consecutive year.
Content: India sets a target of Rs 50,000 crore in defense exports by the year 2030. Agency > New Delhi: India has set a new record in the field of defense exports. According to the Ministry of Defense, a new historic record has been set in defense exports in the financial year 2025-26. During this period, the country's total defense exports increased to Rs 38,424 crore, which shows a strong growth of 62.66 percent compared to the previous financial year. It is noteworthy that India has set a target of Rs 50,000 crore in defense exports by 2030. Along with this, defense production of Rs 3 lakh crore will also be done indigenously. Union Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said that there has been a big increase of Rs 14,802 crore in defense exports. This increase is an indication that the world is relying on India's indigenous defense capabilities and advanced manufacturing. He said that both public sector undertakings and private industries have played an important role in this achievement. The contribution of Indian public sector undertakings in total exports was 54.84 percent, while the share of the private sector was 45.16 percent. Defense Minister Singh said that under the inspiring leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India has written a new success story in the field of defense exports. The Ministry of Defense has achieved another milestone in the financial year 2025-26. Actually, the ministry has fully utilized its capital budget. This budget amount was Rs 1.86 lakh crore. 100 percent of this large capital expenditure was utilized. This is the second consecutive year that the Ministry of Defense has used its entire capital budget. Before this, the capital budget was fully utilized for the first time in many years in the financial year 2024-25. According to the Ministry of Defense, initially, a provision of Rs 1.80 lakh crore was made for capital expenditure, but after the expenditure of the first two quarters and Operation Sindoor, it was increased to Rs 1.86 lakh crore for the armed forces.

Heading: Congress attacks Centre over China’s industrial dominance
Summary:
• Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge accused the Modi government of compromising national interests by allowing Chinese dominance in critical Indian industries.
• Kharge cited rising import dependencies in sectors like pharmaceuticals, EVs, and solar energy since the Galwan clash.
• The Congress leader alleged that the government is facilitating Chinese companies despite ongoing border tensions in Arunachal Pradesh and Ladakh.
Content: NEW DELHI, JUL 9 (PTI): The Congress on Thursday alleged that the Modi government has hurt national interests by letting China “capture” India’s most critical industries and opening more opportunities for the Chinese to “flourish”. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge cited a media report, which claimed that China still powers India’s strategic industries, to attack the government. There was no immediate reaction from the government or the BJP on the Congress’ allegations. He claimed that six years ago, Prime Minister Narendra Modi handed a clean chit to China after 20 brave soldiers made the supreme sacrifice in Galwan. “Our bravehearts chose martyrdom, but Modi Govt has surrendered India’s interests to China,” Kharge alleged in a post on X. He claimed that dependence on China runs through the most critical sectors of India’s economy, which are supposed to define the country’s future. Kharge said since the Galwan clash, imports from China have “exploded” by 101.81 per cent by 2025-26, pushing India’s trade deficit with the neighbouring country to USD 112.1 billion. “China supplied a jaw-dropping 86 per cent of India’s antibiotic imports. Why? China cornered nearly 74 per cent of India’s API, bulk drug, and drug intermediate imports in 2024-25,” he said. Kharge further claimed that 66 per cent of India’s EV component imports still flow from China. Nearly 75 per cent of lithium-ion batteries powering Indian EVs are imported, and the overwhelming bulk of them are Chinese, he said, adding that India imported nearly 93 per cent of permanent magnets from China in 2025-26. “For all the hollow talks by the Modi government on solar energy, it is appalling that China supplied more than 99 per cent of India’s undiffused silicon wafer imports in 2025-26, a near total capture of a sector Modi ji’s claims to champion under Atmanirbhar Bharat. These undiffused silicon wafers are the foundation of our solar cells,” the Congress chief said. “Now, the Modi government has even rolled out the red carpet for his ‘Jhoola Friend’, relaxing restrictions to let four Chinese companies bid for India’s own government power projects. Civil society assertions and reports tell that China continues to encroach on Indian territory in Arunachal Pradesh and Ladakh,” Kharge said. Its role in Pakistan’s actions during Operation Sindoor was acknowledged by none less than the Deputy Chief of Army Staff and stands officially documented, he said. “The Modi government has hurt India’s national interests by letting Beijing capture India’s most critical industries since Galwan. Now they are opening more opportunities for the Chinese to flourish under the lens of his tinted ‘Laal Aankh!’” Kharge said, taking a swipe at Modi.

Heading: 'The world heard the echo of Operation Sindoor', PM Modi said while addressing the Indian community in Melbourne; PM Modi's Australia visit gave a new dimension to defense and energy cooperation: Ministry of External Affairs; Ketan Agrawal murder case: Father's plea for justice to President Droupadi Murmu, request for hearing in Fast Track Court

He also mentioned the Chandrayaan mission, saying, 'You have seen that India landed Chandrayaan on the Moon's South Pole. No other country in the world could do this. The Prime Minister said that the 5G network has expanded rapidly in India and has reached about 90 percent of the country. He also mentioned initiatives like digital transformation, Vaccine Maitri, global crisis relief campaigns, and Aatmanirbhar Bharat. The Ministry of External Affairs stated that both countries agreed to strengthen their strategic partnership in view of the changing global situation. In a special briefing by the Ministry of External Affairs on PM Modi's official visit to Australia, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri said that the main outcomes of today's meeting include the adoption of a joint declaration on defense and security cooperation and the approval of the India-Australia Maritime Security Cooperation Roadmap. This makes it clear that there is a need to take the partnership between the two countries forward according to the changing strategic situation. At the same time, it also shows a shared commitment to strengthen mutual cooperation in the field of defense and security. Both Prime Ministers also agreed that partnerships between industries play a very important role in ensuring reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy supply. For this purpose, a joint statement on energy cooperation was issued, which is also publicly available. In this statement, the commitment of both countries to maintain continuous energy supply between them has been reiterated. The Prime Minister said that India is an important supplier of refined petroleum products to Australia, while Australia has been providing products like coal and natural gas to India for a long time. Pune: In the Ketan Agrawal murder case, the victim's family has written an emotional letter to the President of India, Droupadi Murmu, demanding speedy justice. Ketan's father, Vishal Agrawal, has requested through email to have the case heard in a Fast Track Court and to punish the culprits according to the law. In the letter, Vishal Agrawal wrote that he is not requesting this as a businessman or an influential person, but as a father who has lost his son. He said that his entire family is in deep shock due to the brutal murder of Ketan and every day one question troubles them: when will their son get justice? Mentioning the tragedy in the letter, he said that Ketan's grandfather also passed away within 20 days of Ketan's death. According to him, his father could not bear the shock of his grandson's untimely death and lost his life. In just 20 days, he lost both his son and his father, which shattered the entire family. In the letter addressed to the President, Vishal Agrawal has made it clear that his family is not asking for any special concession or privilege. Their only demand is that the case be heard in a Fast Track Court so that there is no unnecessary delay in justice and the culprits are punished soon.

He also highlighted the reduction of Left-Wing Extremism from 126 districts in eight states to just two districts and lauded the armed forces for the success of Operation Sindoor, saying the Indian Army had eliminated terror camps and high-value targets with precision. Claiming that India was now the world's fastest-growing major economy, Nadda said the country's global stature had risen significantly and called upon people to support the vision of making India a developed nation by 2047. Union Minister G Kishan Reddy, Telangana BJP president N. Ramchander Rao and other BJP leaders attended the programme.

Heading: While shopping for weapon systems abroad, quality of the products should be the buzzword
Summary:
• The article advises Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman against purchasing Chinese J-10 CE fighter jets due to their poor performance in the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.
• It highlights the Indian Air Force's success in destroying Pakistani assets and terrorist camps.
• It warns that reliance on Chinese military hardware could compromise Bangladesh's strategic autonomy.
Content: There are reports that Prime Minister of Bangladesh Tarique Rahman, during his recent visit to Beijing, has also shopped for shopping for Chinese military hardware, though these items have not figured in the list of signed memorandums of understanding as announced in the joint communique issued by the two respective Foreign Ministries and Belt and Road Initiative funds, may be an unwary customer buying products of questionable quality. One hopes that the Prime Minister has kept in view the indifferent performance of some of the Chinese weapon systems deployed in recent combats; particularly during ‘Operation Sindoor’ between India and Pakistan. China wants to sell Dhaka military hardware to make the Bangladesh military dependent on the Chinese military. But Prime Minister Tarique Rahman should think twice before finalizing a planned deal to buy up to 24 J-10 CE fighter aircraft from China. Unlike weapon systems of western origin or Russian weapon systems which have been tested in several recent theatres of battle--Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine, Iran---Chinese weapon systems suffer from a credibility deficit. China has not fought any major battle in the past 50 years. Some of the Chinese weapon systems were used by Pakistan in its short war with India in May 2025, and they have failed across domains. Pakistan gets 81 percent of its military hardware from all-weather friend China. Between 2020 and 2024, about 63 percent of China's total arms exports went to Pakistan. But, in its war with India, Chinese weapon systems like HQ-9 and HQ-16 surface-to-air missiles and J-10 CE aircraft could not prevent Indian attacks on terrorist camps and strategic airfields deep inside Pakistan. Nor could the J-10CE and JF-17 fighter aircraft of Chinese origin do any major damage to Indian installations. The Indian attack on terrorist camps in Pakistan started early on May 7 and by the morning of May 10, the Indian Air Force achieved complete air superiority over a significant portion of the airspace of Pakistan, enabling the IAF to carry out long-range strikes against Pakistani infrastructure at will. The IAF destroyed on the ground about five F-16s, one Erieye Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS), a C-130 transport aircraft and other ground-based facilities. Besides, between May 7 and 10, Indian S-400 air defence systems, of Russian origin, shot down five F-16 and JF-17 fighters. By contrast, the Indian losses, confirmed by wreckage fragments, were restricted to one Rafale, one Mirage 2000 and one Su-30MKI; suffered in the first wave of attacks by Indian fighters on Pakistani terrorist bases early on May 7 when Pakistani J-10CE and JF-17 fighters managed to fire one salvo of PL-15 long-range air-to-air missiles. Pakistan could not support its exaggerated claims about successful hits with satellite imagery or open-source materials. The Indian Rafales did the final job of dismantling camps of terrorists in Pakistan with more powerful Scalp missiles in the war with Pakistan. Thus, with the battlefield records of J-10CE jets yet to be established it may not be prudent for Bangladesh to commit USD 2.2 billion in the purchase of more than 20 such aircraft. It may not be a safe aircraft even. One may recall the death of Captain Yu Xu, the first female pilot of China to fly a J-10C, in an accident while in an exercise with an aerobatic team in November 2016. Beijing has also been actively supporting the indigenous defence industry of Bangladesh through 'Bangladesh' navy set up its first submarine base near Cox's Bazar. Experts warn that if the Bangladesh government makes China the mainstay of its air force too through these acquisitions, then the Bangladesh armed forces will become vulnerable to arm-twisting by Beijing. Last January, Bangladesh Air Force and China Electronics Technology Group Corporation International signed an agreement for establishing near Dhaka a drone manufacturing and assembly plant, with technology transfer.

Heading: Even Caesar did not send a lie to the Senate
Summary: The article discusses the critical importance of truth and accountability from ministers in the Indian Parliament, prompted by a Congress motion against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh for allegedly misleading the House. It emphasizes that furnishing correct information is fundamental to parliamentary democracy and that deliberately misleading Parliament constitutes a breach of privilege. The piece underscores India's civilisational heritage, which stresses truth and righteousness, as foundational to its democratic ideals.
Content: The ensuing Monsoon Session of Parliament is bound to be turbulent, as the Congress seeks privilege proceedings against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, alleging that he misled Parliament over Operation Sindoor about the six soldiers who laid their lives in the line of duty. The Speaker, Lok Sabha, may seek the comments of the Minister or refer it to the Committee on Privileges for enquiry and report. The Speaker has the inherent power to close a matter if satisfied with the explanation tendered. The veracity or otherwise of the allegation will be ascertained after due procedural enquiry. However, the central question is what consequences would visit if a minister deliberately misled the Parliament. The veracity of statements made in the legislature by the members, including ministers, is a fundamental postulate of a deliberative democracy. Ordinarily, it is presumed that the statements made or answers given in Parliament by ministers are sacro sanct, unless proved otherwise. Parliament can function efficiently and effectively as the supreme deliberative body of the nation if accurate and complete information is furnished to it. The Council of Ministers is accountable to the Parliament and the information that they give to Parliament must be correct and complete, without which the doctrine of accountability would become a myth. Accountability of the executive to the legislature is the linchpin of our parliamentary democracy and therefore, it is incumbent upon the ministers to furnish correct and complete and timely information to Parliament and its Committees. Truth, honesty and integrity are quite integral to the proper and effective functioning of Parliament. Not only the ministers and the members, even the witnesses deposing before parliamentary commit tees are deemed to be under oath to speak truth, and complete truth. It is invariably made known to the wit nesses that the deposi tion which they shall make shall be true, that nothing will be con cealed and that, no part of their testimony shall be false. Suppression of truth, giving convoluted answers or to mislead Parliament or its com mittees constitutes a breach of privilege. Therefore, greater responsibility is cast on a minister sworn to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to discharge his duties faithfully and conscien tiously as a Minister for the Union. An inaccuracy or chance mistake may inadvertently creep in the statements made or replies given by a min ister in Parliament. The Rules of Procedure and Directions of Parliament provide that in case any inaccuracy or mistake is detected in any answer given or statement made by a Minister, the same shall be pointed out as soon as it is detected and the mistake recti fied with the permission of the Speaker. There are many instances of the Ministers making the correcting state ments, especially of the answers given to ques tions. But making a misleading statement deliberately or conceal ing information from Parliament constitutes breach of privilege, unless the Minister invokes the plea of national interest. But making a false or delib erately misleading state ment is grossly unethi cal, against sacrosanct parliamentary conven tions and unpardonable. Untruthful or mislead ing statements undermine parliamentary democracy. 'Satyae Meva Jayatae' and 'Yato dharma tato Jaya' are the foremost ideals of India's great civilisa tional heritage. Many consider India as the mother of Democracy, and justifiably, with ref erence to Vedic texts and post-Vedic litera ture. The Indian civili sational texts of great antiquity lay immense stress on truth and right eousness. There are inscriptions in the old Parliament Building taken from the Mahabharata and the Manusmriti reminding that members of the Assembly must speak with righteousness, and the righteousness must be based on truth, and truth is not truth if it leads to deceit.

Heading: 10 yrs after Burhan, how Kashmir's militancy landscape has changed
Summary: Ten years after Burhan Wani's emergence, Kashmir's militancy landscape has significantly transformed, showing a drastic decline in militant and civilian casualties, with only 10 militant killings recorded this year. This positive shift is attributed to effective government action, a crackdown on terror support systems post-2019 abrogation of Article 370, and a change in militant tactics from overt social media presence to more covert operations in dense forests.
Content:
Numbers are indisputable: In 2016, the year after photos of Burhan and his group emerged on social media, 157 militants were killed in Kashmir. This number peaked at 266 in 2018. This year, it's down to 10

•Casualties in Numbers
YEAR | MILITANTS KILLED | SECURITY FORCES KILLED | CIVILIANS KILLED
2016 | 157 | 88 | 56
2017 | 217 | 83 | 54
2018 | 266 | 94 | 88
2019 | 160 | 78 | 42
2020 | 230 | 57 | 37
2021 | 192 | 45 | 36
2022 | 186 | 30 | 30
2023 | 85 | 32 | 11
2024 | 68 | 26 | 32
2025 | 46 | 17 | 28
2026 | 10 | 1 | 1

ON JULY 1, 2015, a picture of 11 young Kashmiri militants, dressed in camouflage, carrying Kalashnikov rifles and posing in a forest, appeared on Facebook. At the centre was Burhan-ud-din Wani, who, shedding anonymity unlike militants before him, chose to broadcast himself and his group on social media and went on to operate in the Valley’s urban areas, particularly south Kashmir.

The images would draw several educated, tech-savvy young men from well-to-do families to follow in Burhan’s footsteps, opening a new chapter in Kashmir’s fight against insurgency and leading to a crisis not seen since the 1990s.

The killing of Burhan in a gunfight on July 8, 2016, triggered protests that shut Kashmir for over three months. As young protestors took to the streets and clashed with police, 55 were killed and thousands injured, with the violence in turn fuelling more recruitments. Many announced they were joining militant ranks publicly, at funeral processions.

Exactly 10 years later, the landscape in the Valley stands decisively transformed, with every key militancy indicator, from the number of active militants to fresh local recruitments to militant attacks and killings, showing a sharp decline.

The numbers are indisputable: In 2016, the year after the social media photos first emerged, 157 militants were killed in Kashmir. The number of foreign operatives, security officials say, hovers around 30.

Less online chatter means security forces have little TE-CHINT to rely on now, the officer adds. “There may be fewer terrorists left, but they have gone silent. The insurgency has become more opaque, harder to penetrate, and harder to track.”

New Delhi

How did Jaish's old network fail?
According to intelligence agencies,

Will Jaish's existence survive on the internet?

In recent months, due to the vigilance of security forces and strict patrolling on the border, its activities in Jammu and Kashmir have become negligible.

Heading: 5 Dead in Wayanad Landslide, Search for Buried Continues; Indonesia to Buy BrahMos from India, 20 Agreements Signed Including Defense, Agriculture
Summary: A landslide in Wayanad, Kerala, has resulted in 5 deaths and 7 missing, with ongoing rescue operations by various agencies including NDRF and state administration.
